source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 14 (PDF 18-44, printed 15-41); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 14 (Simple Harmonic Motion), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Simple harmonic motion is a special type of oscillatory motion in which a restoring force always pulls the object:

options.text: along the tangent of a circle

blocks.explanation: In S.H.M the restoring force always pulls the object back towards its mean position (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: a special type of oscillatory motion where a restoring force always pulls the object back

blocks.prompt: 2 Which of the following is given in the chapter as an example of periodic motion in nature?

options.text: Motion of the Moon around the Earth
A car moving on a straight road
A ball rolling down a slope

blocks.explanation: Motion of the Earth around the Sun and of the Moon around the Earth are natural periodic motions (Introduction box).

book_ref.quote: Like motion of Earth around the Sun, The motion of moon around the Earth

blocks.prompt: 3 Oscillatory motion is best described as:

options.text: motion in a straight line with constant speed
rotation about a fixed axis only
a to and fro periodic motion about a mean position

blocks.explanation: Oscillatory motion is a to and fro motion about the mean position that repeats after equal intervals of time (14.1).

book_ref.quote: Oscillatory motion is a to and fro motion about its mean position

blocks.prompt: 4 When sound waves travel through air, the air molecules:

options.text: move along with the wave to the listener

blocks.explanation: Air molecules oscillate when sound waves travel through air; it is one of the listed examples of oscillatory motion (14.1).

book_ref.quote: Air molecules oscillate when sound waves travel through air.

blocks.prompt: 5 When an oscillating body is displaced from its mean position, the force that brings it back is called:
blocks.explanation: A restoring force brings the displaced body back to its equilibrium position and causes oscillation (14.1).

book_ref.quote: then there is restoring force which brings it back to its equilibrium position

blocks.prompt: 6 One complete round trip (cycle) of a vibrating body about its mean position is called:
blocks.explanation: One complete round trip (cycle) about the mean position is one vibration (Terms).

book_ref.quote: One complete round trip (cycle) of vibrating body about its mean position is called vibration

blocks.prompt: 7 For a pendulum swinging between extreme positions A and B, one vibration is the motion:

options.text: from A to the mean position
from A to B and back to A
from the mean position to B

blocks.explanation: Motion of the bob from A to B and back from B to A is one vibration (Terms).

book_ref.quote: motion of bob of pendulum from A to B and back from B to A is one vibration

blocks.prompt: 8 The distance of a vibrating body from its mean position at any instant is called:
blocks.explanation: Instantaneous displacement x is the distance from the mean position at any instant (Terms).

book_ref.quote: The distance of a vibrating body from its mean position at any instant, is called instantaneous displacement

blocks.prompt: 9 The magnitude of the maximum displacement of a vibrating body on either side of its mean position is its:
blocks.explanation: Amplitude x₀ is the magnitude of the maximum displacement on either side of the mean position (Terms).

book_ref.quote: The magnitude of the maximum displacement of the vibrating body on either side of its mean position

blocks.prompt: 10 According to the chapter, a wave of greater amplitude carries:
blocks.explanation: Amplitude measures the energy carried by a wave: greater amplitude, greater energy (Terms).

book_ref.quote: The greater the amplitude of the wave, greater will be the energy carried by the wave

blocks.prompt: 11 A pendulum has amplitude 6 cm. The distance covered by the bob in one complete vibration is:
blocks.explanation: In one vibration the bob goes mean → extreme → mean → other extreme → mean: 4x₀ = 4 × 6 cm = 24 cm.

book_ref.quote: If x₀ is the amplitude of simple pendulum

blocks.prompt: 12 The time taken to complete one vibration is called:
blocks.explanation: Time period T is the time taken to complete one vibration; its SI unit is the second (Terms).

book_ref.quote: Time period is defined as the time taken to complete one vibration or one cycle

blocks.prompt: 13 A body completes 12 vibrations in 3 s. Its frequency is:
blocks.explanation: f = n/t = 12/3 s = 4 Hz (Terms).

book_ref.quote: Frequency is defined as the number of vibrations or oscillations (n) completed by the vibrating body in one second

blocks.prompt: 14 A body on a spring makes 12 vibrations in 3 s. Its time period is:

book_ref.quote: A fish connected to a spring makes 10 vibrations in 20 seconds

blocks.prompt: 15 One hertz is defined as:
blocks.explanation: The unit of frequency is the hertz; one hertz is one oscillation per second (Terms).

book_ref.quote: One hertz is defined as one oscillation per second

blocks.prompt: 16 The dimension of frequency is:
blocks.explanation: Frequency = 1/T, so its dimension is [T⁻¹] (Terms).

book_ref.quote: The dimension of frequency is [T⁻¹].

blocks.prompt: 17 Angular displacement per unit time is called:
blocks.explanation: Angular frequency ω = θ/t is angular displacement per unit time (Terms).

book_ref.quote: Angular displacement per unit time is called angular frequency

blocks.prompt: 18 The SI unit of angular frequency is:
blocks.explanation: The SI unit of angular frequency is rad s⁻¹ and its dimension is [T⁻¹] (Terms).

book_ref.quote: The SI unit of angular frequency is rad s⁻¹ and its dimension is [T⁻¹].

blocks.prompt: 19 A body vibrates with frequency 5 Hz. Its angular frequency is about:
blocks.explanation: ω = 2πf = 2π × 5 = 10π ≈ 31.4 rad s⁻¹ (Terms).

book_ref.quote: Now for one revolution θ = 2π radian

blocks.prompt: 20 The time period T is related to the angular frequency ω by:
blocks.explanation: T = 1/f = 2π/ω (Terms).

book_ref.quote: Time period in terms of frequency f and angular frequency ω is expressed as:

blocks.prompt: 21 A particle in S.H.M has angular frequency 4 rad s⁻¹. Its time period is about:
blocks.explanation: T = 2π/ω = 2π/4 = π/2 ≈ 1.57 s (frequency 0.637 Hz), as in Example 14.1 with ω changed.

book_ref.quote: A particle executing simple harmonic motion has an angular frequency of 2 rad s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 22 A particle in S.H.M has angular frequency 4 rad s⁻¹. Its frequency is about:

book_ref.quote: The frequency is approximately 0.318 Hz, and the time period is approximately 3 seconds.

blocks.prompt: 23 Which of these is NOT listed as an example of oscillatory motion?

options.text: A bullet moving in a straight line
Wings of a bird during flying

blocks.explanation: Tuning fork, swing and birds' wings are listed oscillations; a bullet in a straight line does not move to and fro (14.1).

book_ref.quote: The wings of birds during flying.

blocks.prompt: 24 Simple harmonic motion is a type of:

options.text: motion in a straight line with constant velocity

blocks.explanation: S.H.M is a type of oscillation or vibratory motion produced under the action of a restoring force (14.2).

book_ref.quote: Simple harmonic motion is a type of oscillation or vibratory motion produced under the action of restoring force.

blocks.prompt: 25 For S.H.M, the restoring force must be:

options.text: proportional to the square of the displacement

blocks.explanation: A necessary condition: the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position (14.2).

book_ref.quote: The restoring force shall be directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position.

blocks.prompt: 26 In Hooke's law F = −kx for an oscillating spring, k depends on:

options.text: the nature of the material of the spring

blocks.explanation: k is the spring constant that depends on the nature of the material of the spring (14.2).

book_ref.quote: The force and displacement should follow Hooke's law

blocks.prompt: 27 In the condition a ∝ −x for S.H.M, the negative sign shows that the acceleration is:

options.text: directed away from the mean position

blocks.explanation: The negative sign indicates that acceleration is directed towards the mean position (14.2).

book_ref.quote: the negative sign indicates that acceleration is directed towards mean position

blocks.prompt: 28 The restoring force in S.H.M depends only on the:
blocks.explanation: F = −kx: the restoring force depends only on the displacement, not on the inertia (14.2, book correction).

book_ref.quote: The restoring force is not proportional to the inertia (mass) of the body; it depends only on the displacement

blocks.prompt: 29 What carries an oscillating body past its mean position?
blocks.explanation: The body must have inertia, which carries it past the mean position (14.2).

book_ref.quote: The body must have inertia, which carries it past the mean position

blocks.prompt: 30 The motion of the recorder needle of an electrocardiogram is periodic but not S.H.M because:

options.text: its restoring force is not always proportional to displacement
it has no restoring force at all

blocks.explanation: Not all periodic vibrations are S.H.M; in an ECG the restoring force is not always proportional to displacement (14.2 box).

book_ref.quote: An electrocardiogram traces the periodic pattern of a beating heart

blocks.prompt: 31 A spring of constant 200 N m⁻¹ is stretched 4 cm. The restoring force on the body is:

options.text: 8 N away from the mean position

blocks.explanation: F = −kx = −200 × 0.04 = −8 N; the minus sign means towards the mean position (Eq. 14.2).

book_ref.quote: Consider a body of mass 'm' attached with a spring of spring constant 'k' lying on smooth horizontal surface

blocks.prompt: 32 A mass on a spring, released at A, crosses the mean position O because of:
blocks.explanation: On release the body moves to O and crosses it due to inertia, reaching B (14.3).

book_ref.quote: it will move towards 'O' and will cross the mean position O due to inertia

blocks.prompt: 33 A 0.5 kg mass on a spring of constant 40 N m⁻¹ is at x = +3 cm. Its acceleration is:

book_ref.quote: The negative sign shows that acceleration and displacement are always in opposite direction

blocks.prompt: 34 The mathematical form of simple harmonic motion is:
blocks.explanation: From a = −(k/m)x, a ∝ −x: acceleration proportional to displacement and directed to the mean position (14.3).

book_ref.quote: It shows that acceleration of the body executing S.H.M is always directly proportional to the displacement

blocks.prompt: 35 The spring constant k depends upon:

options.text: the physical shape and structure of the spring
the mass attached to the spring

blocks.explanation: k depends on the nature (physical shape and structure) of the spring (14.3).

book_ref.quote: where 'k' is spring constant depending upon the nature (physical shape and structure of a spring)

blocks.prompt: 36 For a mass-spring system, the angular frequency ω is:
blocks.explanation: Comparing a = −(k/m)x with a = −ω²x gives ω² = k/m, so ω = √(k/m) and f = (1/2π)√(k/m).

book_ref.quote: T is the reciprocal of f = (1/2π)√(k/m)

blocks.prompt: 37 The time period of a mass-spring system is:
blocks.explanation: T = 1/f and f = (1/2π)√(k/m), so T = 2π√(m/k) (book correction to the printed √(k/m)).

book_ref.quote: T is the reciprocal of f = (1/2π)√(k/m), so m/k comes under the root

blocks.prompt: 38 If the mass on a spring is made four times, its time period becomes:
blocks.explanation: T = 2π√(m/k) ∝ √m; √4 = 2, so the period doubles.

book_ref.quote: A heavier mass gives a longer period.

blocks.prompt: 39 A 2 kg mass oscillates on a spring of constant 50 N m⁻¹. Its time period is about:

book_ref.quote: The last line should read T = 1/f = 2π√(m/k)

blocks.prompt: 40 Which is given as a real-world application of the S.H.M principle?
blocks.explanation: Pendulum clocks, musical instruments and vehicle suspension systems use the S.H.M principle (Point to ponder).

book_ref.quote: Real world applications that utilize S.H.M principle include

blocks.prompt: 41 The first pendulum clock was patented in 1656 by:
blocks.explanation: Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens patented the first pendulum clock in 1656 (box).

book_ref.quote: Christiaan Huygens patented the first pendulum clock in 1656

blocks.prompt: 42 A simple pendulum consists of a small heavy bob suspended by a:
blocks.explanation: A small heavy bob hangs from a rigid support by a light inextensible string (Simple pendulum).

book_ref.quote: A simple pendulum consists of a small heavy solid bob of mass m suspended from a rigid support

blocks.prompt: 43 For a simple pendulum displaced by angle θ, the restoring force is provided by:
blocks.explanation: mg cosθ is balanced by the tension; mg sinθ provides the restoring force towards the mean position.

book_ref.quote: The component mg sinθ provides the necessary restoring force towards mean position

blocks.prompt: 44 In a simple pendulum, the component mg cosθ is cancelled by:
blocks.explanation: mg cosθ and the tension T act along the string in opposite directions and cancel; there is no motion along the string.

book_ref.quote: the component mg cosθ and tension T are along the same line but in opposite direction

blocks.prompt: 45 For small angles of a simple pendulum, sinθ may be replaced by:
blocks.explanation: For small angles sinθ ≈ θ with θ in radians, giving a = −gθ (book correction: not 0).

book_ref.quote: For small angles sinθ ≈ θ (θ in radians)

blocks.prompt: 46 The approximation x ≈ arc length S for a simple pendulum holds when the angle is about:
blocks.explanation: x is very nearly equal to S when the angle is small, about 10° or less.

book_ref.quote: when the angle is small (about 10 or less)

blocks.prompt: 47 For a simple pendulum of small amplitude, the acceleration is a =
blocks.explanation: a = −(g/ℓ)x (Eq. 14.7); g/ℓ is constant, so a ∝ −x and the motion is S.H.M.

book_ref.quote: This is the mathematical from of S.H.M and it is concluded that the motion of a simple pendulum is S.H.M.

blocks.prompt: 48 A simple pendulum is 2.45 m long. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², its time period is about:

book_ref.quote: The above expression shows that the time period of simple pendulum is directly proportional to the square root

blocks.prompt: 49 The time period of a simple pendulum (small amplitude) is independent of:
blocks.explanation: T = 2π√(ℓ/g) does not contain m; it is independent of the mass of the bob and the amplitude.

book_ref.quote: The time period of motion of the pendulum is independent of the mass m of the bob and amplitude.

blocks.prompt: 50 If the length of a simple pendulum is made four times, its time period becomes:
blocks.explanation: T ∝ √ℓ; √4 = 2, so T doubles.

book_ref.quote: inversely proportional to the square root of acceleration due to gravity

blocks.prompt: 51 A second pendulum is one whose time period is:
blocks.explanation: A pendulum that completes one vibration in two seconds (T = 2 s) is a second pendulum.

book_ref.quote: A pendulum that completes one vibration in two seconds

blocks.prompt: 52 If a pendulum is taken to a place where g is smaller, its time period:
blocks.explanation: T = 2π√(ℓ/g) ∝ 1/√g; smaller g gives a longer period.

book_ref.quote: A pendulum is shifted from Lahore to Karachi will its time period change?

blocks.prompt: 53 The word 'pendulum' comes from a Latin word meaning:
blocks.explanation: Pendulum is derived from the Latin word pendulus, meaning hanging (box).

book_ref.quote: Pendulum is derived from Latin word Pendulus means hanging.

blocks.prompt: 54 A pendulum 0.80 m long has a time period of 1.80 s. The value of g at that place is about:

book_ref.quote: The simple pendulum can be used to determine the gravitational acceleration at a particular location.

blocks.prompt: 55 Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², the length of a pendulum with time period 1.5 s is about:

book_ref.quote: Also find its frequency at a place where the value of g is taken to be 9.8 m s⁻²

blocks.prompt: 56 While measuring the time period of a simple pendulum, a small amplitude is used because:

options.text: sinθ ≈ θ holds only for small angles, so T = 2π√(ℓ/g) applies
a large amplitude makes the bob heavier
g is zero at large amplitude
the string stretches only at small amplitude

blocks.explanation: The derivation of T = 2π√(ℓ/g) uses sinθ ≈ θ and x ≈ S, which are true only for small angles.

book_ref.quote: While measuring the time period of a simple pendulum it is recommended to take small amplitude, why?

blocks.prompt: 57 A pendulum of fixed length is taken from the Earth to the Moon, where g is smaller. Its time period:
blocks.explanation: T = 2π√(ℓ/g); smaller g on the Moon gives a longer period.

book_ref.quote: Would the time period of a simple pendulum be same on Earth and moon

blocks.text: 14.4 Simple Harmonic Motion and Uniform Circular Motion

blocks.prompt: 58 When a particle moves in a circle with uniform angular velocity, its projection on a diameter:
blocks.explanation: The projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter executes S.H.M (14.4).

book_ref.quote: It has been observed that when a particle moves in a circular path, its projection on diameter of the circle executes S.H.M.

blocks.prompt: 59 In the turntable experiment, which part executes S.H.M?

options.text: the shadow of the ball on the screen

blocks.explanation: The ball moves in uniform circular motion; its shadow on the screen oscillates in S.H.M (14.4).

book_ref.quote: A beam of light casts a shadow of the ball on the screen

blocks.prompt: 60 For a particle moving on a circle of radius x₀ with angular velocity ω, its linear velocity is directed:
blocks.explanation: The linear velocity at P is along the tangent, vₚ = rω (Quantitative analysis).

book_ref.quote: Its linear velocity at point P is along the tangent

blocks.prompt: 61 The instantaneous displacement of the projection Q of a particle on a circle is:
blocks.explanation: From triangle POQ, x/x₀ = cos θ with θ = ωt, so x = x₀ cos ωt (Eq. 14.11).

book_ref.quote: the angle which the radius OP sweeps out in time t is θ = ωt

blocks.prompt: 62 The instantaneous velocity of the projection Q equals:
blocks.explanation: Q vibrates horizontally, so its velocity is the horizontal component of vₚ (Instantaneous velocity).

book_ref.quote: the line PR is the horizontal component of velocity vₚ of the particle

blocks.prompt: 63 A body in S.H.M has ω = 5 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 0.10 m. Its speed at x = 0.06 m is:

book_ref.quote: Eq. (14.13) should read v = ω√(x₀² − x²)

blocks.prompt: 64 A body in S.H.M has amplitude 0.04 m and ω = 15 rad s⁻¹. Its maximum speed is:
blocks.explanation: v_max = x₀ω = 0.04 × 15 = 0.60 m s⁻¹, at the mean position (Eq. 14.14).

book_ref.quote: It may be noted that at mean position x = 0 and velocity is maximum.

blocks.prompt: 65 The expressions for time period, displacement, velocity and acceleration of the projection are:

options.text: also applicable to the particle moving in the circle
true only at the mean position
never true for any real body

blocks.explanation: These expressions, true for the projection, are also applicable for the particle moving in a circle (box).

book_ref.quote: The expressions such as time period, displacement, velocity and acceleration which are true for projection

blocks.prompt: 66 The acceleration aₚ of a particle in uniform circular motion is directed:

options.text: towards the centre of the circle

blocks.explanation: aₚ is centripetal: directed towards the centre; its horizontal component is the acceleration of Q.

book_ref.quote: Acceleration aₚ of the particle at point P is directed towards the centre of the circle

blocks.prompt: 67 A particle moves on a circle with period 2 s. The acceleration of its projection at x = 0.1 m is about:
blocks.explanation: ω = 2π/T = π rad s⁻¹; a = −ω²x = −π² × 0.1 ≈ −0.99 m s⁻² (Eq. 14.15).

book_ref.quote: This expression is the mathematical condition of S.H.M

blocks.prompt: 68 A body in S.H.M has amplitude 0.02 m and ω = 10 rad s⁻¹. The magnitude of its maximum acceleration is:
blocks.explanation: |a|max = x₀ω² = 0.02 × 10² = 2 m s⁻², at the extreme positions.

book_ref.quote: As particle is moving in the circle with uniform angular frequency ω

blocks.prompt: 69 A 0.25 kg mass on a spring of constant 25 N m⁻¹ is at x = 0.04 m. Its acceleration is:
blocks.explanation: ω² = k/m = 25/0.25 = 100; a = −ω²x = −100 × 0.04 = −4 m s⁻² (as in Example 14.3, new values).

book_ref.quote: A 0.2 kg mass is attached to a spring with a spring constant of 10 N m⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 70 The angle θ = ωt that specifies the displacement and the direction of motion of a point in S.H.M is called:
blocks.explanation: The angle θ = ωt that specifies x and the direction of motion is the phase (14.5).

book_ref.quote: The angle θ = ωt which specifies the displacements x as well as the direction of motion

blocks.prompt: 71 Phase is the quantity that shows the:

options.text: state of motion of an oscillator

blocks.explanation: Phase shows the state of motion of an oscillator (14.5).

book_ref.quote: Phase is the quantity which shows the state of motion of an oscillator.

blocks.prompt: 72 The phase constant φ in x = x₀ cos(ωt + φ) depends on the:
blocks.explanation: The value of φ depends on the displacement and velocity of the particle at t = 0.

book_ref.quote: The value of φ depends on the displacement and velocity of the particle at t = 0.

blocks.prompt: 73 In x = x₀ cos(ωt + φ), the time-varying quantity (ωt + φ) is called the:
blocks.explanation: (ωt + φ) is the phase; the constant φ alone is the phase constant (14.5).

book_ref.quote: The time varying quantity (ωt + φ), is called the phase of the motion.

blocks.prompt: 74 For x = x₀ cos ωt (φ = 0), at t = 0 the point is at:
blocks.explanation: With φ = 0, x = x₀ at t = 0: the point starts at an extreme position (Fig. 14.8 a).

book_ref.quote: With θ = ωt, Eq. (14.17) is x = x₀ cos ωt, the case φ = 0 drawn in Fig. 14.8 (a).

blocks.prompt: 75 For x = x₀ cos ωt, the point is at the mean position at:
blocks.explanation: At t = T/4 and 3T/4 (θ = π/2, 3π/2) the point is at the mean position (Fig. 14.8 a).

book_ref.quote: the point is at the extreme positions. At t = T/4 and 3T/4

blocks.prompt: 76 For x = x₀ cos(ωt + 90°), at t = 0 the point is at:
blocks.explanation: cos 90° = 0, so x = 0 at t = 0: the point is at the mean position (Fig. 14.8 b).

book_ref.quote: If φ = 90°, then Eq. (14.18) becomes:

blocks.prompt: 77 Two oscillating systems with a phase difference of 180° are said to oscillate:
blocks.explanation: A phase difference of 180° means the systems oscillate out of phase (14.5).

book_ref.quote: When the phase difference between two oscillating systems is 180°

blocks.prompt: 78 Two oscillating systems are in phase when their phase difference is:
blocks.explanation: Phase difference 0° or 360° means oscillating in phase (14.5).

book_ref.quote: When phase difference between oscillating systems is 0° or 360°

blocks.prompt: 79 A body oscillates as x = 0.1 cos ωt with T = 1.2 s. Its displacement at t = 0.2 s is:

book_ref.quote: Where x is instantaneous displacement, x₀ is maximum displacement

blocks.prompt: 80 For x = x₀ cos ωt, what phase angle corresponds to t = T/8?

book_ref.quote: Putting t = 0, T/4, T/2, 3T/4, ...., we obtain a graph

blocks.prompt: 81 From x = x₀ cos ωt, the particle has its maximum displacement x₀ at the:
blocks.explanation: Maximum displacement x₀ occurs at the extreme position (14.6).

book_ref.quote: This shows that the particle will have maximum displacement (x₀) at extreme position.

blocks.prompt: 82 The magnitude of the maximum velocity of a particle in S.H.M is:
blocks.explanation: v_max = x₀ω at the mean position; it is zero at the extremes (14.6).

book_ref.quote: The velocity of the particle is maximum (i.e., v = x₀ω) at the mean position

blocks.prompt: 83 For x = x₀ cos ωt, the velocity with its sign is:
blocks.explanation: For x = x₀ cos ωt the velocity is v = −x₀ω sin ωt, so the velocity graph falls first.

book_ref.quote: For x = x₀ cos ωt the velocity is v = −x₀ω sin ωt, so it falls first

blocks.prompt: 84 In S.H.M the acceleration is maximum at the:
blocks.explanation: |a| = x₀ω² is maximum at the extreme positions and zero at the mean position (14.6).

book_ref.quote: The acceleration will be maximum (i.e., x₀ω²) at the extreme positions

blocks.prompt: 85 The phase difference between acceleration and displacement in S.H.M is:
blocks.explanation: Since a = −ω²x, acceleration and displacement are always opposite: phase difference π (book correction).

book_ref.quote: acceleration and displacement are always opposite: their phase difference is π

blocks.prompt: 86 The phase difference between velocity and displacement in S.H.M is:
blocks.explanation: Velocity and displacement differ in phase by π/2 (14.6).

book_ref.quote: The phase difference between velocity and displacement is π/2.

blocks.prompt: 87 A body moves as x = 0.05 cos ωt with ω = 8 rad s⁻¹. Its acceleration at t = 0 is:

book_ref.quote: Putting x = x₀ cos ωt, we have:

blocks.prompt: 88 When the displacement of a body in S.H.M is zero, its speed is:
blocks.explanation: x = 0 at the mean position, where the speed is maximum (graphs of Fig. 14.9).

book_ref.quote: The graphical representations of displacement, velocity and acceleration of a body executing SHM

blocks.prompt: 89 The potential energy of a body in S.H.M is due to its:
blocks.explanation: P.E. is on account of the displacement; K.E. is due to the velocity (14.7).

book_ref.quote: Its potential energy is on account of its displacement from mean position

blocks.prompt: 90 In S.H.M without frictional forces, the total energy:

options.text: is zero at the mean position

blocks.explanation: K.E. and P.E. vary, but the total energy remains constant without unbalanced frictional forces (14.7).

book_ref.quote: the total energy at any instant remains constant in the absence of unbalanced frictional forces

blocks.prompt: 91 A spring of constant 300 N m⁻¹ is stretched to 2 cm. The average force over this stretch is:

book_ref.quote: Thus, average value of force from the mean position to the extreme position is:

blocks.prompt: 92 The work done in stretching a spring of constant 300 N m⁻¹ by 2 cm is:

book_ref.quote: When the spring is stretched to its maximum displacement x₀, work is done on the spring

blocks.prompt: 93 The work done in stretching the spring is stored as:
blocks.explanation: The work done is stored as elastic potential energy, P.E. = ½kx² (14.7).

book_ref.quote: This work done on the mass attached to a spring is stored in terms of potential energy

blocks.prompt: 94 The potential energy of a mass-spring oscillator is maximum at:
blocks.explanation: P.E. = ½kx² is zero at x = 0 and maximum at x = ±x₀ (Eq. 14.22).

book_ref.quote: It is clear from Eq. (14.22) that the potential energy of oscillator is zero at x = 0

blocks.prompt: 95 The kinetic energy of a mass-spring oscillator at displacement x is:
blocks.explanation: K.E. = ½mv² = ½k(x₀² − x²) (Eq. 14.26).

book_ref.quote: Hence, at any instant where the displacement is x, the kinetic energy of mass attached to spring is given by

blocks.prompt: 96 In terms of mass and angular frequency, the total energy of an oscillator is:
blocks.explanation: Putting k = mω² into ½kx₀² gives T.E = ½mω²x₀² (book correction to Eq. 14.29).

book_ref.quote: Eq. (14.29) should read T.E = ½mω²x₀²

blocks.prompt: 97 If the amplitude of a mass-spring oscillator is tripled, its total energy becomes:
blocks.explanation: T.E = ½kx₀² ∝ x₀²; 3² = 9.

book_ref.quote: it is proved that total energy of mass spring system is constant and is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude

blocks.prompt: 98 A spring of constant 100 N m⁻¹ oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Its total energy is:

book_ref.quote: When displacement = x₀; Force = F = kx₀

blocks.prompt: 99 At x = x₀/2, what fraction of the total energy of an oscillator is kinetic?
blocks.explanation: P.E./T.E = x²/x₀² = 1/4, so K.E. = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4 of the total.

book_ref.quote: The energy oscillates between K.E. and P.E., but their sum remains constant.
